name: St Peter's Basilica
label: St Peter's Basilica
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/244159210: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Peter's Basilica' (268 m across).
notes: Also spot 3 on the Rome map (the owner, 2026-11-05: a landmark may be on more than one map).

text.description:
St Peter's Basilica is the great Renaissance church of Vatican City, and its central dome dominates the Rome skyline. The building is approached across St Peter's Square, which has two sections, an oval and then a trapezoid, both wrapped in tall colonnades. The wide façade, with its giant columns, stretches across the far end. Two statues of Saints Peter and Paul, each 5.55 metres tall, stand on the steps in front.

That is why it photographs so well. The colonnades lead the eye towards the façade, and the dome rises behind it as a clear finishing shape. Building work began on 18 April 1506 and finished on 18 November 1626, and several famous architects shaped the design, including Bramante, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno. Bernini designed the square and many of the fittings. It is also the largest church in the world by interior measure.

The phone icon on the map is about 290 m east of the subject. At that distance the whole building fits in the frame with room for the open space and people in front of it. Take one wide shot to show the scale, then zoom in for the dome and the statues. Keep your phone level so the tall columns do not lean. If the square is busy, wait a moment for a gap, or use people walking across it to show how big the place is. Right next to it: Michelangelo's Pietà. Right next to it: Dome of St Peter's (rooftop view).
text.geographic_location: St Peter's Basilica stands in Vatican City, at the western end of St Peter's Square. It lies west of the River Tiber, near the Janiculum Hill.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is the Risorgimento/S. Pietro tram stop (tram 19), about 9 minutes on foot from the basilica, which lies to the south-west of the stop. From the Metro, Cipro (Metro line A) is about 12 minutes on foot (the basilica lies to the south-east of the station) and Ottaviano (Metro line A) about 15 minutes (to the south-west). The phone icon on the map is about 290 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole façade and dome together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the colonnades and the open square in the frame, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and the statues on the steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 290 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the centre of the façade and dome with the middle vertical line. Use the horizontal lines to keep the rooftop level and the columns upright. Leave some open ground and people in the lower part of the picture to give a sense of scale. Then zoom in for a tighter shot of the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the stonework. If you use telephoto, hold the phone steady with both hands and elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives warm light on the stone, but go early in the day if you want fewer people in the square.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the basilica is a working place of worship, so check the official site before you go for entry and dress rules.

name: St Peter's Square and the colonnade
label: St Peter's Square
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'St. Peter's Square'.
notes: UK 'st peter's square' alone is mostly Manchester, so only 'vatican' and the Italian name count.

text.description: St Peter's Square is the huge open space in front of St Peter's Basilica, and it is easy to photograph because its shapes are so clear. Two curving Tuscan colonnades, four columns deep, wrap around an oval of paving. At the centre stands the red granite Vatican obelisk, 25.5 m tall and about 41 m to the cross on top, raised on bronze lions. It was moved here in 1586, and Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the square around it between 1667 and 1676. Two matching fountains, dated 1613 and 1675, sit either side of the obelisk. Together they give you symmetry, lines and scale in one view. Look down as well: travertine lines run across the paving, and circular stones mark where the obelisk's shadow falls at noon through the year. For a simple, balanced shot, stand at the phone icon on the map and face west, with the obelisk in the middle and the basilica behind it. Put a fountain or a curve of columns at one edge to show the size of the place. Then turn around for the colonnade on its own, where the rows of columns make strong repeating lines. The square is very large and often busy, so keep your phone steady, take a few frames, and let people in the foreground show the scale.
text.geographic_location: In Vatican City, in the large forecourt directly in front of St Peter's Basilica, with the colonnades curving around it to the north and south.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Risorgimento/S. Pietro (tram 19), about 7 minutes on foot, with the square to the south. From Ottaviano (Metro line A) it is about 13 minutes on foot, with the square to the south, and from Cipro (Metro line A) about 16 minutes on foot, with the square to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the colonnades, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the obelisk with the basilica behind it. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the obelisk, the bronze lions or details of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the obelisk on the centre line so the symmetry reads clearly. Keep the horizon level and the columns upright. Include one of the fountains or a curve of the colonnade at the edge of the frame for depth. For a second shot, stand against the colonnade and shoot along the rows of columns.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the basilica façade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the pale stone or sky looks too bright. Panorama mode can work for the full curve of the square if you turn slowly and keep the phone level. Avoid moving people in the middle of a panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the light at the time you visit, as it changes how the façade and colonnades look. Early in the day it is usually quieter too. Evening, when the lights come on, suits night mode if you can brace your phone against something solid.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but access conditions can change, so check the official Vatican site before you go.

name: Vatican Museums
label: Vatican Museums
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.

text.description:
The Vatican Museums are the public museums of Vatican City, and they hold one of the biggest art collections anywhere. The collection numbers roughly 70,000 works, with about 20,000 on display. The museums began with one sculpture, Laocoön and His Sons, which was found in Rome in January 1506. Pope Julius II bought it and put it on show a month later. The route leads you to the Sistine Chapel, decorated by Michelangelo, and to the rooms painted by Raphael. In 2024 the museums had 6.8 million visitors, so expect company.

For a phone photographer the appeal is the rooms themselves as much as the artworks. The Sala Rotonda is shaped like a miniature Pantheon, with mosaic floors and statues around the edge. The Braccio Nuovo has a wide arched roof with skylights. The Octagonal Court has held famous classical statues since the early 1500s. Each of these gives you strong lines, repeating shapes and a clear sense of scale.

Step back from crowds when you can, and wait a few seconds for a gap rather than chasing every angle. Look for symmetry down a long gallery, then move in for one statue or a patch of mosaic. Keep your phone steady and avoid flash. Check the official site before you go for current photography rules, as they can differ from room to room and can change.
text.geographic_location: The museums are inside Vatican City, about 440 m east of Cipro (Metro line A), next to the Cortile del Belvedere and the sculpture galleries described in the sources. The Sistine Chapel is the last room on the visitor route.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Cipro (Metro line A), about 7 minutes on foot, with the museums to the east. You can also take tram 19 to Risorgimento/S. Pietro, about 8 minutes on foot, with the museums to the west. Ottaviano (Metro line A) is a little further, about 10 minutes on foot, with the museums to the south-west. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for long galleries and domed rooms such as the Sala Rotonda, so you fit in the ceiling and floor. Use the default lens (1x) for most shots of statues and room corners. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a face, a mosaic or ceiling decoration.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand in the middle of a gallery doorway or room and shoot along its length, so the architecture frames the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the room's walls and arches so they stay straight. Put a statue or archway in the centre of a symmetrical room, and keep the floor mosaic or the skylights in the frame for depth. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or let people in the frame give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue or wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright skylights and windows don't wash out. In dim rooms, hold the phone steady against your body and let night mode finish before you move. Avoid flash.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early or late in the day, when it may be less busy, and check the official site for opening times. Rooms with skylights, such as the Braccio Nuovo, are likely to look best in good daylight.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed museum complex, so check the official site before you go for entry, queues and photography rules.

label: Vatican Gardens

text.description: The Vatican Gardens are the green heart of Vatican City. They cover about 23 hectares, roughly half of Vatican City, and fill most of the western side. Lawns, flower beds and clipped topiary sit alongside fountains, sculptures, an artificial grotto devoted to Our Lady of Lourdes and a patch of woodland of about 3 hectares. Some medieval fortifications and buildings from the 9th century onwards are scattered among them. The gardens began as orchards and vineyards in medieval times. Pope Nicholas III enclosed the area with walls in 1279, and a major re-landscaping followed in the early 16th century under Pope Julius II. For a phone camera, the appeal is in the layers: neat green lawns, sculpted hedges, stone fountains and tall pines and cedars in one frame. Pope Francis opened the gardens to the public in 2014, but visits are with a guide, either as an individual or in a pre-formed group, so you will be moving at the group's pace. Use that to your advantage by taking quick, simple shots as you walk, rather than planning elaborate compositions. Keep the lens clean, look for a foreground such as a flower bed or a fountain, and let the lawns and trees fill the background. Always check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements and photography rules.
text.geographic_location: The gardens lie in the west of Vatican City, in Rome, at about 41.9031° N, 12.4506° E. They are bounded by stone walls on the north, south and west sides.
text.directions_text: Take Metro line A to Cipro; the gardens are to the south-east of the station, about 9 minutes on foot. Valle Aurelia (Metro line A) is a little further, with the gardens to the east, about 12 minutes on foot. Alternatively, take tram 19 to Risorgimento/S. Pietro, with the gardens to the south-west, about 12 minutes on foot. Visits to the gardens are guided, so check the official site before you go. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for general views of lawns and paths. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for open lawns and long vistas, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for fountains, sculptures and details of the topiary.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 230 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use a flower bed, hedge line or path as a foreground. Keep the horizon level and let trees or stonework frame the sides. Take a few steps between shots rather than relying on zoom alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the greenery or stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if bright sky is washing out the leaves. Use portrait mode for close shots of statues or flowers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the lawns and stone. Check the official site for visiting arrangements before you go.

text.access_note: The gardens are open to visitors only with a guide, individually or in a pre-formed group, so check the official site before you go.

name: Raphael Rooms and the School of Athens
label: Raphael Rooms
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (2026-11-11T01:00).

text.description:
The Raphael Rooms are a suite of four reception rooms on the second floor of the Apostolic Palace, now part of the Vatican Museums. Pope Julius II commissioned the young Raphael, who came from Urbino, around 1508 or 1509 to redecorate them completely. The rooms overlook the south side of the Belvedere Courtyard. Raphael and his workshop covered the walls with frescoes, and after Raphael died in 1520 his assistants finished the last room. The rooms are the Sala di Costantino, the Stanza di Eliodoro, the Stanza della Segnatura and the Stanza dell'Incendio del Borgo.

The rooms photograph well because everything is painted on a grand scale. Figures, architecture and colour fill the walls from floor level to ceiling. The Sala di Costantino is the largest of the rooms. In the Stanza di Eliodoro, painted between 1511 and 1514, Raphael used dramatic, theatrical lighting effects in the paintings themselves, which gives you strong shapes to frame.

For a phone, think in two steps. First take one wide shot to show how a painted wall meets the room around it. Then take one or two closer shots of a single group of figures. Other visitors may be in the frame, so be patient. The rooms may be busy, so stay calm and steady. Wipe your lens before you go in, as a smudge shows badly on a bright painted wall.
text.geographic_location: The rooms are in the Apostolic Palace inside Vatican City, on the second floor of the Vatican Museums, just north of the Sistine Chapel. They overlook the south side of the Belvedere Courtyard.
text.directions_text: From Metro line A, get off at Ottaviano, about 11 minutes on foot, with the rooms to the south. Cipro on Metro line A is a little further, about 14 minutes on foot, with the rooms to the south-east. The rooms are reached from inside the Vatican Museums, so check the official site for the visitor entrance and route before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view of a wall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the room is too tight to fit a whole wall in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for faces and small details high on the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pick a spot a few steps back from the wall, near the middle of the room, so you can include the frame and the floor.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line them up with the edges of the painted wall so the architecture does not lean. Hold the phone level and square to the wall. Take one wide shot of the whole wall, then a closer shot of a single group of figures. If heads cross the frame, wait a moment for a gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the fresco to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright areas look washed out. Avoid flash, and avoid night mode unless the light is very dim, as it can blur if you move. Brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the official site for opening details before you go. Indoor light is mostly steady, so the time of day matters less for your exposure settings.

text.access_note: These rooms are inside the Vatican Museums, so check the official site before you go for entry, photography rules and opening details.
claims_not_in_sources: The rooms may be busy with other visitors.

name: Pinecone Courtyard
label: Pinecone Courtyard
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Cortile del Belvedere'.

text.description:
The Pinecone Courtyard (Cortile della Pigna) is the upper part of the long Belvedere Courtyard that Donato Bramante began designing in 1505 to link the Vatican Palace with the Villa Belvedere. It is a calm, formal space: grassed sections laid out in a pattern that matches 16th-century engravings, long wings on either side, and at the far end a huge half-domed niche. The niche was completed by Pirro Ligorio in the 1560s, and it is the largest of its kind built since antiquity. Standing in it is the courtyard's namesake, a big bronze pinecone. The courtyard also looks like a separate space because a library wing built across the original court in the late 1500s split it in two. In 1990 a sculpture of two concentric spheres by Arnaldo Pomodoro was placed in the middle of the courtyard.

This works well for phone photos because the straight lines of the wings and the great niche lead the eye in. The shiny sphere gives you a modern foreground against the Renaissance backdrop, and the pinecone makes a good close subject. Try one wide shot with the niche as the centrepiece, then a closer one of the sphere with the niche behind it. Look out for reflections in the sphere's surface, and wait a moment for people to move out of the frame. The courtyard is enclosed, so you may find the light uneven, with bright sky above and some shaded areas beside the wings.
text.geographic_location: In the Vatican, at about 41.9042° N, 12.4547° E, on the upper terrace of the Belvedere Courtyard, between the long wings that now house the Vatican Museums collections and the Vatican Library.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Risorgimento/S. Pietro on tram 19, about 6 minutes on foot, with the courtyard to the south-west. Alternatively, take Metro line A to Ottaviano (about 11 minutes on foot, courtyard to the south-west) or Cipro (about 11 minutes on foot, courtyard to the south-east). Allow extra time for queues and for the walk inside the museum complex. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the sweep of the wings and the great niche. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the sphere, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bronze pinecone and details of the niche.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, turn to face the great niche and shoot along the length of the space.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the niche with the middle of the frame so the symmetry of the wings looks tidy. Place the Pomodoro sphere in the foreground and keep the niche behind it. For the pinecone, use zoom rather than walking off the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pinecone or the sphere to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. Check the sphere's reflection before you press the shutter, as you may catch yourself in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the visit or later in the day usually means fewer people in the frame. On a bright day the wings may cast some shade, so check your highlights.

text.access_note: The courtyard is part of the Vatican Museums complex, so access may be ticketed or restricted: check the official site before you go.

name: Bramante Staircase (spiral staircase)
label: Spiral Staircase
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3057821: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The modern Momo staircase is the one most photographed; both are named so.

text.description:
The name Bramante Staircase covers two double-helix stairs in the Vatican Museums. The original was built in 1505 to a design by Donato Bramante, and it stands in a square tower of the Belvedere palace. The one most visitors actually walk down is the modern version from 1932, designed by Giuseppe Momo and inspired by Bramante's. It is a pair of ramps winding round the outer wall of a stairwell about fifteen metres wide, with open space at the centre. Because there are two separate ramps, people going up and people coming down never meet.

It photographs well because of the repeating curves. The ornate metal balustrade sweeps round and round, and a canopy above lets in light that falls down the well. Looking over the rail gives a strong spiral pattern, and you can fill the frame with it in seconds. The modern stair sits at the end of the museum visit, and everyone leaves by this route, so you will pass it without a detour. The original 1505 stair, with its 36 granite columns, is not generally open to the public, though specialist tours do visit.

For phone photography, keep your hands steady and take a few frames as you descend, since the view changes with each turn. Leave a little space around the edges so you can straighten or crop later. Expect other visitors to be moving through, so be patient and shoot between groups. Check the official site before you go for any rules on photography inside the museums.
text.geographic_location: The staircase is inside the Vatican Museums, in the Pio-Clementine Museum area of Vatican City. The original 1505 stair stands in a tower of the Belvedere palace; the modern stair is also in the Pio-Clementine Museum.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Risorgimento/S. Pietro (tram 19), and the staircase is to the west of it, about 5 minutes on foot. Ottaviano (Metro line A) is about 8 minutes on foot, and the staircase lies to the south-west of that station. Cipro (Metro line A) is about 9 minutes on foot, with the staircase to the east. Milizie/Angelico (tram 19) is about 11 minutes on foot, with the staircase to the south-west. The staircase is inside the museums, so you reach it as part of your visit, at the end. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole spiral and the open well. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of a few turns. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details of the balustrade and the curve of the ramp.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Pause at the rail on one of the upper turns and aim down across the well. Keep to the flow of people and don't block the ramp.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the central opening up with the middle of the frame, so the curves repeat evenly on both sides. Hold the phone level to keep the spiral from tilting. For a second shot, point along the ramp to show the curve of the balustrade leading away.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the stairwell to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the light from above doesn't wash out the detail. If the light is low, use night mode and hold still. If you want a short moving clip of the descent, try Live Photos.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The canopy lights the stair from above, so it works at any time the museums are open. Expect other visitors on the stair at any time, so be patient.

text.access_note: The modern staircase is inside the Vatican Museums at the end of the visit, and the original 1505 stair is not generally open to the public, so check the official site for entry details and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The Vatican Museums may have entry details and rules on photography, so visitors should check the official site.
Standing at the rail on an upper turn and aiming down across the well gives a good view of the spiral.
The canopy light makes the stair workable for photos at any opening hour.

name: Gallery of Maps
label: Gallery of Maps
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/10774102205: the OpenStreetMap point 'Galleria delle Carte Geografiche'.

text.description:
The Gallery of Maps is a long corridor in the Vatican, lined with painted maps of Italy. Pope Gregory XIII commissioned it in 1580. The friar and geographer Ignazio Danti drew the designs, and the work took three years, 1580 to 1583. Forty panels run along a gallery about 120 m long. Each panel shows a region of Italy, usually with a perspective view of its main city. The Apennines act as a dividing line: one wall shows the regions facing the Ligurian and Tyrrhenian seas, and the other shows those facing the Adriatic. The maps are said to be roughly 80% accurate, which is impressive for the 16th century.

It photographs well because of the repetition. The same panels, framing and vaulted ceiling run away from you in a long line, which gives a strong sense of depth even on a small screen. The ceiling was decorated by a group of Mannerist artists including Cesare Nebbia and Girolamo Muziano, so there is plenty to look at above you as well as beside you.

For a good phone shot, stay near the wall rather than the middle of the walkway and try one wide view down the whole corridor. Then move in for a single map, such as the view of a port city at one end. Expect other visitors in the frame. Wait a few seconds for a gap, or include people to show the scale. Wipe your lens before you start, as a smudge will show in the shot.
text.geographic_location: The gallery is in the Vatican, at the spot marked on the map for the 'Galleria delle Carte Geografiche'. It is a long, narrow hall rather than an open outdoor space.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is Risorgimento/S. Pietro (tram 19). From there the gallery is about 6 minutes on foot, to the south-west. From Ottaviano (Metro line A) it is about 11 minutes on foot, to the south-west. From Cipro (Metro line A) it is about 10 minutes on foot, to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view down the corridor. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole painted ceiling and both walls. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a single map or a city view without leaning towards the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Choose a spot along the corridor with a clear view along its length, and keep to the side so you don't block other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the ceiling up with the middle of the frame, so the corridor looks straight and symmetrical. Hold the phone level to keep the walls from leaning. For a detail shot, fill the frame with one map and keep its edges parallel to the screen.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-bright part of a map to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly if the ceiling looks washed out. Hold your breath and keep your elbows in when you press the shutter. Interior light can make photos blurry.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the official site before you go for visiting times.

text.access_note: Check the official site for entry and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Photography rules, such as a ban on flash, may apply inside the gallery.
The gallery is often busy with visitors.
The corridor has bright overhead and ceiling lighting that can wash out a phone exposure.

name: Michelangelo's Pietà
label: Pietà
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/10578527910: the OpenStreetMap point 'Pietà'.

text.description:
Michelangelo's Pietà shows Mary holding the body of Jesus after he has been taken down from the cross. It is carved from Carrara marble and dates from 1498–1499. It stands in St Peter's Basilica, in the first chapel on the north side after you come in, where it has been since the 18th century. It was made for a French cardinal's funeral chapel in the older church that stood on the site.

It photographs well because the whole group forms a calm pyramid, with Mary's head at the top and her wide, heavy drapery spreading out to the base. Mary looks very young, and the faces and folds of cloth are what draw the eye, so a close, simple frame suits it. It is also the only work Michelangelo ever signed. His name is carved on the sash across Mary's chest, though it is too small to read clearly in a phone photo from a distance.

The sculpture sits behind a bulletproof glass screen, which was replaced and updated in November 2024 ahead of the 2025 Jubilee. The screen can pick up reflections, so move a little to one side and watch for bright patches before you shoot. Take a few frames, then pick the sharpest. The basilica can be dimly lit and busy, so hold the phone steady with both hands and keep your elbows against your body.
text.geographic_location: Inside St Peter's Basilica in Vatican City, in the first chapel on the north side just after the main entrance (about 41.9023, 12.4546).
text.directions_text: Start at the Risorgimento/S. Pietro stop on tram 19. The basilica is to the south-west, about 8 minutes on foot. From Cipro (Metro line A) it is about 13 minutes on foot, heading south-east. From Ottaviano (Metro line A) it is about 14 minutes on foot, heading south. Once inside the basilica, look for the first chapel on the north side after the entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole chapel, then try telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the two figures. Because of the glass, telephoto lets you stay back and still get a close view. Ultra-wide (0.5x) is better kept for the basilica interior around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand as near the front of the chapel as is allowed, slightly off to one side rather than dead centre.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pyramid shape of the group in the middle, with Mary's head near the top of the frame. Keep the sculpture upright and avoid cutting off the base. For a second shot, go closer with telephoto on the faces and the folds of Mary's drapery.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble (the face of Jesus or Mary) to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white stone keeps its detail. Night mode can help in dim light, but hold very still, as it needs a steady phone. Check your photo for reflections in the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when the basilica is quieter so you have a clear spot at the front of the chapel. Check the official site for visiting times.

text.access_note: This is a place of worship, and entry rules, dress code and any photography rules may apply, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The glass screen can cause reflections in photos.
The basilica interior can be dimly lit and crowded.
The signature is too small to read clearly in a phone photo taken from a distance.
St Peter's Basilica may have a dress code and photography rules.
Quieter times at the basilica make it easier to reach the front of the chapel.

name: Dome of St Peter's (rooftop view)
label: St Peter's Dome
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/244159210: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Peter's Basilica' (268 m across).
notes: The view from the top; ticketed climb (check the official site).

text.description: The subject is the great dome of St Peter's Basilica, and the phone icon on the map sits right at it, so the picture here is the view looking out from the dome rather than a shot of it from the square. The dome is one of the largest in the world and dominates the Roman skyline, so from up here you look out over St Peter's Square, the rooftops of Rome and the city beyond. The square is a forecourt in two parts, an oval and a trapezoid, both ringed by tall colonnades. From above, that shape reads clearly and makes a strong, graphic foreground for a phone photo. The basilica was designed principally by Bramante, Michelangelo and Maderno, with the square and fittings by Bernini. Building began on 18 April 1506 and finished on 18 November 1626. That is more than a century of work behind the stonework around you. For phone photos, keep the horizon level and use the gridlines to line up the colonnades and rooflines. Tap on the distant skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky looks washed out. If you are shooting through railings or a window, hold the lens close to the barrier and keep your hand steady. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the same view can look very different at 0.5x and at 3x. Expect to share the space with other visitors.
text.geographic_location: In Vatican City, at the middle of St Peter's Basilica, under its central dome, which stands at the end of St Peter's Square on the west side of the River Tiber. The basilica is close to the Janiculum Hill and Hadrian's Mausoleum.
text.directions_text: The nearest stop is the tram 19 stop Risorgimento/S. Pietro, about 9 minutes on foot from the phone icon on the map, with the dome lying to the south-west. Alternatively, take Metro line A to Cipro (about 12 minutes on foot, dome to the south-east) or to Ottaviano (about 15 minutes on foot, dome to the south-west). Once you reach St Peter's Square, the basilica and its dome are impossible to miss. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the square, the colonnades and the sweep of Rome's rooftops. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view. Use the telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant domes and towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the top or bottom third line. Use the curve of the colonnades as a leading shape and keep the lines straight. Take one wide shot, then a tighter zoomed shot of a single landmark. Take a few frames, since people move through the view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the distant rooftops to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly to keep the sky from burning out. If the view is hazy, a Live Photo can give you a choice of frames. Wipe your lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light and gentler shadows over the rooftops than midday sun. Check the official site for visiting times before you plan.

text.access_note: Access to the dome and any viewing level may be ticketed, timed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
